title: Theme 1 Synthesis and Fresh Evidence Check
intro: Revisit three ideas in a new combination. Block C evidence checkpoint.

terms.def: Combining earlier ideas into a new explanation, using unworked pairings rather than repeating corrected answers.

body: Three threads run the whole theme. Oral tradition carries law governments still use, from treaty intent to court evidence. Collective rights live at the group level, from the hoarding lesson to the Charter worry. And every agreement has at least two readings, from wampum councils to Meech Lake.

Fresh check, unworked pairing: Carpenter's land ethic says use and sharing, never ownership. The Two Row Wampum models two vessels travelling side by side, neither steering the other. Explain in three sentences how both sources support the same claim about what treaties were for, naming each source and one detail from each.

The three threads braid into one argument for the final answers. Law lives in story and ceremony, so oral evidence counts. Rights live in peoples, so individuals exercise them through nations. Agreements live in relationship, so every reading must ask whose understanding is on the page. Hold all three at once and no booklet question can surprise you.

A last word on evidence, the course's through-line from Lesson 1. Courts weigh oral history with written records, negotiators weigh spoken promises against printed texts, and your answers weigh examples against claims. In each forum the rule is identical: name the source, quote the detail, explain the link.

example.title: Block C checkpoint
example.text: You should now be able to define Section 35, recount Meech Lake and Charlottetown, define Aboriginal title, apply the rights test, name the three negotiating partners, compare two self-government models, and complete both critical responses.

check.prompt: How do Carpenter and the Two Row support the same claim about treaties?
check.sample: Sample response: Carpenter's sharing ethic shows land held for use, and the Two Row shows parallel self-direction, so both support treaties as relationship agreements rather than land sales.
